items.question: How do you understand the difference in consciousness between people with locked-in syndrome and people in a coma?

items.answer: So it depends on who you ask, and I'll try to channel the two camps if you want. Locked-in—make sure that everyone knows—people who essentially lost the ability to move their body but their brain is intact. That's the summary, and there are examples of those people. They have thoughts, they can imagine things, but they rarely can even communicate to the outside world that they are there, and we're lucky to even know that they're totally conscious just inside a statue, which is their body. So they have consciousness. They feel things. They can think thoughts. When we manage to communicate with them, they express the full variety of things humans can experience. So they are totally conscious. The other extreme are people in a coma. So those are people basically who had a car accident, got injured, and for all purposes are essentially vegetables. For a while we thought that they feel nothing. They basically are dead with some biological that keeps them alive, but they're not really there to think. Recently there have been studies that show that potentially there is someone there who might even experience things. The famous work by this Belgian scientist showed that you can take those people and essentially pinch them with a kind of needle, and you look at the insula part of the brain that responds to pain, and it is active. So they seem to experience pain.

items.question: What do you see as the best role for AI in education?
items.object: AI as a personalized learning tool within teacher-guided education
items.answer: I think that for the most part, AI is helpful to us in the sense that students can go to class and learn one thing, and then they can go home and ask AI to supplement the material in their language and in their way. So when I studied physics for undergrad years ago, it would look like this. A professor would enter the classroom, turn their back on us, open a huge blackboard, start scribing equations, speak to himself, and we would sit there and copy from the whiteboard and hope that something would sink. I think Feynman said that in physics, you don't understand things, you get used to them. This was the thing. We just kept copying with the hope that something is going to sink. But back in the days when I was learning about something called a Fourier transform, this not complex idea but an idea that's abstract, I think I didn't really understand it. I knew how to calculate it and I knew what it meant, but I didn't really see it. And a year and a half ago I asked one of the AIs, I forget which one it was, to explain it to me again. And it not only explained it to me in a nice way, it also said, “Here are videos that illustrate that beautifully.” And I went to their videos and the videos were suddenly showing in computer graphics, 3D animations, this idea, and now I got it. So I always knew it, but now I get it. And this is a great thing because AI knows me. It knows that I'm a visual person and it will help me to just see it in 3D. And now each kid from my class can take the class and learn what is the topic that's important, and then go home and ask AI in their language, in their style, to give them videos and graphics and stories and whatever examples. So they come back the next time they know it, and I can trust AI to do this job. The teachers are still there to chart the road. They're like Moses. They take the Jews in the desert, but each person and each mini tribe gets to plot their own course of knowledge. And I think that is the best version we can do. And it means that there's a lot more burden on us to make sure that everyone is aligned. We have to ask the question the following class and say, “Hey, everyone did the homework, everyone's here and so on. Sally, did you get it your way? Adam, did you get it your way?” But at the same time, we cannot control what the way is.
